Not that I disagree that they're going in a wrong direction, but I think it's easier to say that than to suggest a 'right' direction.

Microsoft made a lot of their previous revenue from selling software to manufacturers. Consumers wouldn't buy new operating systems, but they would buy new computers and that new computer came with an already licensed copy of a new OS. But hardware iteration rates have dramatically slowed. If you don't play modern games a computer bought today, or anytime in the past several+ years, will last you indefinitely. They were banking everything on an infinite upgrade cycle which is obviously short sighted but we see all sorts of companies do this - Apple today is still doing this exact same thing.

What they've done with Windows 10 was raw desperation. And that's further limited their options. They just basically completely relegated themselves to business-to-business as they just completely destroyed their brand trust among many consumers.

Here's an example of a missed opportunity:

Imagine working on a desktop PC. You get an email with a PDF attachment - a coworker wants you to proofread it. Open the PDF, then reach up to the screen and flick it to your tablet. It's now open on your tablet. Pick up the tablet, mark up the PDF, save it, then flick it back to your desktop to return to your coworker.

Got a video on your laptop you want to show the wife? Flick it to the XBox and it's on the TV.

How about using a 4k tablet as a second monitor for your PC? Or as an input control for your XBox? Look at the TV listings on your tablet, click on a movie and open its IMDB page, then flick it to the XBox and it tunes to that channel so you can watch.

Microsoft had the power to do that, but they wasted it rewriting half of Windows and I don't even know what they were doing.

But I think Ballmer didn't have the vision to make Microsoft disruptive, and I suspect Nadella doesn't have the cojones.
